description: With Valeri Ponzo and Gian Basili. Our first visit to this cool park.

Seen on the Green Dragon Trail.

Spent several hours hiking around LLELA. I ended up getting a bit turned around on my last trail of the day, the Bittern Marsh Trail and was running late on getting out by 7PM. Ranger Rob saw me walking towards the exit and was nice enough to give me a ride out of the park.

Wish I would've been able to blacklight here as some areas seemed pretty green and there was a lot of insect activity.

Observed while visiting Grapevine for an education conference (SREB 2022). I was invited by the National Geographic education team to give a presentation on using iNaturalist in the classroom and had a great time presenting and also learning from the Nat Geo team.

I mostly stuck to the area near the Gaylord Texan hotel as there were plenty of woods to explore and blacklight at. I did also go on an iNat marathon on Friday the 22nd when I met sambiology and he took me to two really great spots: Cross Timbers Park and Tandy Hills.
I also went to LLELA shortly after to round off the day.

description:
Field Journal Entry #1 

Date: 2/4/24
Start time: 9:45 am
End time: 10:30am
Location: Redstone Pines
Weather: Very sunny, no wind, about 30 degrees F
Habitats: Large eastern pine stand with a young decisdous forest next to it. Deciduous stand has oaks, black Cherry, and lots of understory shrubs, and lots of in invasive buckthorn. 

The pines in the Redstone Pines stand are very tall, I would guess more than 50ft. All the birds I could observe were at the very tops of the trees and I unfortunately did not have a pair of binoculars with me. So, I ID the birds I saw today mainly by listening to their songs and calls. It was a very bright and sunny day, so there was lots of action, especially with the Black-capped chickadees. I think for next time, I definitely need to bring binoculars to make sure I can really see the birds I’m trying to observe. 

Here are the birds I saw and/or heard:
- Black-capped chickadee
- Tufted titmouse 
- Red or white breasted nuthatch
- American goldfinch
Merlin ID were able to back me up with  a couple of sound recordings!
I also believe I saw/heard some downy or hairy woodpeckers. At the near tops of the pines, I could see some robin-sized birds climbing vertically along the trees, and they were making short chirps similar to the sounds I could play on Merlin for the downy and hairy woodpeckers. 

There were A LOT of chickadees. Even on my walk to and from the redstone pines, they were just everywhere and so so loud! While in the redstone pines, the chickadees were mostly doing their alarm calls instead of the simple fee-bee call. Perhaps they were extra territorial because there were so many? I noticed that their flight pattern is quite ‘bouncy’. They would quickly go up and down from branch  to branch, and often perch along the vertical trunks. They flap their wings very fast in chunks/bursts at a time. It was very easy for me to lose track of the same bird. I think this is quite useful to their habitat niches, as they are flocking in trees and the quick bouncy movement makes it easier to tree/branch hop and can be quite disorientating to predators, especially with their black and white head.

In addition to the usual Gray Squirrels, the Tufted Titmice and Northern Cardinals along the trail are tame; clearly, lots of people feed them. Multiple titmice and cardinals flew toward me and perched expectantly as I walked past. Had I had food for them, I'm sure that the titmice would have fed from my hand.

description:
A solo visit to check on the Sparkleberry bushes. They're just starting to bloom, so the next 1-3 weeks should be great for hairstreaks. There were lots of lupines, pawpaws, and especially Lyreleaf Sages blooming. Butterflies were scarce but I photographed four species of moths. Variable Dancers were common; I quit photographing them after the 4th one encountered. I walked the usual trails in clockwise order, since I wanted to visit the main Sparkleberry patch first. I used my camera to take macro photographs, and after about 15 minutes of last using it, I realized that my phone was not in my pocket. I remembered where I last used it and back-tracked my path right to the phone.

Surprisingly, there were few vehicles in the parking lot at my arrival, and no mother truckers on the mound. (Did somebody from FWC or SWFWMD finally tell the mother truckers that a state preserve is not appropriate for them to run their r/c vehicles over the area?). Several people were crossing Aripeka Road to go swimming in the pond to the south. 

The weather at my arrival was sunny and 79 degrees ("feels like" 82) -- both temperatures seemed low -- with a light breeze. The weather when I left was one degree warmer, which again seemed too low. I left at 1717 after exactly 3 hours and headed home.
place_guess: Florida, Pasco, Aripeka area, Aripeka Sandhills Preserve

I've wanted to see a Tufted Titmouse since I started birding 10+ years ago. I tried recording it but it was pretty windy and after I got out my phone, it flew further off. 

Next day, we are returning home and driving by so we gave it another try. Again, the bird is calling loudly from the neighborhood. Suddenly, it occurs to me to pull up the song of the Tufted Titmouse and bingo. By time I realized what I was hearing, it again grew quiet and we needed to move on.

Still haven't seen one, though.

description:
I participated in the Ohio Wildlife Observation: Solar Eclipse 2024 with the intent to watch my domestic poultry behavior with my young grandchildren. We predicted that they would think evening was coming and return to their coop. Our outcome was as we thought. The rooster called hens together, nothing crazy, and they slowly moved back to their coop area as normal, and waiting for it to become darker and go in. But it didn't get dark but became "morning" again. So, they ran back to normal range area. Nothing crazy was observed only the rooster who is general calm was a little aggressive. While doing this project with poultry, we did observe the songbirds' behavior. As the eclipse was close and getting dusk out, we notice the songbirds that sing at evening were sing. When the eclipse was ending, (in between), the songbirds that sing in the morning began. There was a very brief moment when it sounded busy, like both songs were happening at the same time. Then everything was calm. Again, like the poultry nothing crazy and behavior was expected.
(Recording of birds singing 15 minutes after eclipse.)

description:
Colt Creek butterfly count with Linda Cooper, Rob Epstein, and Delia Smith in our party. There were three other parties. We drove mostly unpaved roads in the southern portion of the state park, east to its boundary at the powerline cut (the state park is much larger than I realized; at nearly 6,000 acres!). The weather at the start was sunny and 77 degrees ("feels like" 77) with a light breeze. Deer Flies, mosquitoes, and humidity were non-existent. Owing to the drought, butterfly numbers were mostly low, but we had fairly high diversity (35 species for our party). Multiple records of the same species, especially Southern Skipperling (7 records, plus 22 records of 7 other skipper species) and Carolina Satyr (15 records), represent different individuals. Identified by sound

This organism was observed perched on a branch in a tree on a cloudy, humid day, with temperatures above 80°F. The bird was identified by its distinctive vocalizations. The environment consisted of trees with dense underbrush nearby, providing cover and protection as the bird foraged on the ground.

Class: Aves - Endothermic vertebrates characterized by feathers, beaks, and the ability to lay hard-shelled eggs
Order: Passeriformes - Perching birds with three forward-facing toes and one backward-facing toe, well-suited for gripping branches
Family: Paridae - Small to medium-sized birds known for their short, stout bills, rounded wings, short legs, and strong feet

The presence of feathers and a beak, along with the ability to lay hard-shelled eggs, confirms its classification as Aves.
As a member of the Passeriformes order, the bird has specialized feet with three forward-facing toes and one backward-facing toe, ideal for gripping and perching on tree branches.
The bird's distinctive tufted crest on its head is a key feature, helping to distinguish it from other species within the Passeriformes order.
The bird was seen calling to others and flying between trees, engaging in typical social and foraging behaviors.

As a vertebrate, the bird's skeletal structure is adapted for flight, with a lightweight yet strong frame that includes pneumatic bones for reduced weight and increased efficiency during flight. Its keeled sternum provides an anchor for the flight muscles, enabling powered, sustained flight. The bird’s diapsid skull, featuring two temporal fenestrae, supports the beak and helps reduce skull weight. Fused bones are common in Aves, including the synsacrum (a fusion of the sacral, lumbar, and some tail vertebrae) and the furcula (wishbone), which stabilize the body during flight.
The presence of a syrinx allows this bird to produce its distinctive calls and songs. The syrinx is located at the junction of the trachea and bronchi, enabling the bird to produce complex vocalizations that are crucial for communication, whether to mark territory, attract mates, or coordinate with other birds. The ability to produce such vocalizations is a key characteristic of Passeriformes and is essential to the social behavior of many species within this order.

The weather was clear and cool with calm winds at the start, becoming sunny and hottish with a light breeze by the end. This checklist covers solely the ravine overlook area. The flycatcher was first heard calling at 0844 and was viewed intermittently until 0910, when we lost it. It was seen later (not photographed by us, so I don't have the times) then disappeared for a few more hours before being found again (by others; we didn't see it) from around 1330 to around 1400. I got several decent photographs and one call note on audio. We left the ravine area at 1245 and drove a short distance to Sheelar Lake. Other taxa: (Sherman's) Fox Squirrel, Eastern Fence Lizard; several Lone Star ticks :(

description: North Pinellas Christmas Bird Count with Mia Majetschak. While Mia covered her yard and a small park, I drove to Philippe Park (during daylight!). The temperature at the start was sunny, 55 degrees ("feels like" 53) and breezy (NNW at 12 mph). The tide was high. Mia and I met at the boat ramp around 0820 and after scoping the (nearly birdless) northwestern part of Tampa Bay, we walked the trails away from the shoreline. The damage to the park from Hurricanes Helene and Milton was relatively light, but several large oaks (decades old) were toppled. We did well here, finding owls (the incubating Great Horned Owl, a local celebrity) and three Eastern Screech-Owls that responded to our playback to attract landbirds -- I don't know that I have ever had 3 Eastern Screech-Owls respond to playback at any one spot before -- and numerous passerines, including a Western Tanager, the highlight of the CBC. (I got one headless and several out-of-focus photos. Fortunately Mia refound the tanager on 22 Dec and got definitive photos. We left at 1220 and got lunch before returning later to survey the southern half of the park.
